etymology: Webster (1828): [Gr. See Monarch.] The Greek letters are not printed in the live text; this entry does not supply them.
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines monarchy as “a state or government in which the supreme power is lodged in the hands of a single person.” He separates “absolute or despotic monarchies” from “limited monarchies,” where the king’s power is “limited by a constitution, or by fundamental laws.” Scripture records Israel’s demand, “make us a king to judge us like all the nations” (1Sa 8:5), and God’s word to Samuel, “they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them” (1Sa 8:7). The law had already bounded any king: “Thou shalt in any wise set him king over thee, whom the LORD thy God shall choose” (Deu 17:15). Every throne answers to the one who says, “By me kings reign” (Pro 8:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): MONARCHY, government with supreme power in one person; absolute or limited by a constitution or fundamental laws; a kingdom or empire.
webster_full: MON'ARCHY, noun [Gr. See Monarch.]

1. A state or government in which the supreme power is lodged in the hands of a single person. Such a state is usually called an empire or a kingdom; and we usually give this denomination to a large state only. But the same name is sometimes given to a kingdom or state in which the power of the king or supreme magistrate is limited by a constitution, or by fundamental laws. Such is the British monarchy Hence we speak of absolute or despotic monarchies, and of limited monarchies.
A free government has a great advantage over a simple monarchy
2. A kingdom; an empire.
scriptures: And said unto him, Behold, thou art old, and thy sons walk not in thy ways: now make us a king to judge us like all the nations.
And the LORD said unto Samuel, Hearken unto the voice of the people in all that they say unto thee: for they have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them.

Thou shalt in any wise set him king over thee, whom the LORD thy God shall choose: one from among thy brethren shalt thou set king over thee: thou mayest not set a stranger over thee, which is not thy brother.
Pro 8:15
By me kings reign, and princes decree justice.
corruption_summary: Monarchy is now heard mostly as a ceremony or a relic; Webster’s question of whether a king’s power is limited by law is lost.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster drew the line that mattered: absolute monarchy against a monarchy “limited by a constitution, or by fundamental laws.” Modern speech treats the word as pageantry and forgets that the real question is whether the ruler stands under law.

Scripture puts every king under God. Israel’s king was to be chosen by the LORD and kept from lifting his heart above his brethren; the request for a king “like all the nations” was counted as a rejection of God’s own reign (1Sa 8:5–7).
roots_summary: One ruler holding supreme power, absolute or bounded by law, always under God.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): supreme power lodged in a single person.
Webster: absolute or despotic, or limited by a constitution.
Israel asked for a king like all the nations (1Sa 8:5).
The king must be one whom the LORD chooses (Deu 17:15).
By me kings reign (Pro 8:15).

pos: n. (government by the principal persons of a state)
etymology: Webster (1828): [Gr. best, and to hold or govern.]
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines aristocracy as “a form of government, in which the whole supreme power is vested in the principal persons of a state; or in a few men distinguished by their rank and opulence.” He adds that oligarchy “is usually applied to a corrupted form of aristocracy.” The Greek root means rule by the best. Scripture names what “best” must mean in a ruler: “able men, such as fear God, men of truth, hating covetousness” (Exo 18:21), “wise men, and understanding, and known among your tribes” (Deu 1:13). Rank and wealth are not the test; “When the righteous are in authority, the people rejoice” (Pro 29:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): ARISTOCRACY, government with supreme power in the principal persons of a state, or a few distinguished by rank and opulence; oligarchy its corrupted form.
webster_full: ARISTO'CRACY, noun [Gr. best, and to hold or govern.]

A form of government, in which the whole supreme power is vested in the principal persons of a state; or in a few men distinguished by their rank and opulence. When the supreme power is exercised by a small number, the government is called an oligarchy. The latter word however is usually applied to a corrupted form of aristocracy
scriptures: Moreover thou shalt provide out of all the people able men, such as fear God, men of truth, hating covetousness; and place such over them, to be rulers of thousands, and rulers of hundreds, rulers of fifties, and rulers of tens:
Deu 1:13
Take you wise men, and understanding, and known among your tribes, and I will make them rulers over you.
Pro 29:2
When the righteous are in authority, the people rejoice: but when the wicked beareth rule, the people mourn.
Jas 2:1
My brethren, have not the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, with respect of persons.
corruption_summary: Aristocracy now names a social class of birth and wealth, not a form of government, and the root sense of rule by the best is gone.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster wrote of a form of government. Modern use means a hereditary upper class, a set of titles and estates, or any elite.

He already saw the danger: power held by “a few men distinguished by their rank and opulence” slides into oligarchy. Scripture forbids respect of persons in judgment and asks for rulers who fear God and hate covetousness (Exo 18:21; Jas 2:1).
roots_summary: Rule by the few called best; Scripture defines best by the fear of God, not by rank.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): supreme power in the principal persons of a state.
Webster: oligarchy is a corrupted form of aristocracy.
Able men, such as fear God (Exo 18:21).
When the righteous are in authority, the people rejoice (Pro 29:2).
usage: a few men distinguished by their rank and opulence

pos: n. (accusation of a public officer for maladministration)
etymology: Webster (1828) enters IMPE’ACHMENT without an etymology note; this entry does not supply one.
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines impeachment as “an accusation or charge brought against a public officer for maladministration in his office.” In the United States, he notes, “it is the right of the house of representatives to impeach, and of the senate to try and determine impeachments.” The principle is older than any constitution: rulers are accountable, and charges must be proved. “At the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established” (Deu 19:15). Paul applies the same rule to elders: “Against an elder receive not an accusation, but before two or three witnesses” (1Ti 5:19). Samuel invited it of himself: “witness against me before the LORD” (1Sa 12:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): IMPEACHMENT, an accusation against a public officer for maladministration; the act of impeaching; censure, calling in question.
webster_full: IMPE'ACHMENT, noun Hinderance; impediment; stop; obstruction.

1. An accusation or charge brought against a public officer for maladministration in his office. In Great Britain, it is the privilege or right of the house of commons to impeach, and the right of the house of lords to try and determine impeachments. In the U. States, it is the right of the house of representatives to impeach, and of the senate to try and determine impeachments. In Great Britain, the house of peers, and in the U. States, the senate of the U.States, and the senates in the several states, are the high courts of impeachment
2. The act of impeaching.
3. Censure; accusation; a calling in question the purity of motives or the rectitude of conduct, etc. This declaration is no impeachment of his motives or of his judgment.
4. The act of calling to account, as for waste.
5. The state of being liable to account, as for waste.
scriptures: One witness shall not rise up against a man for any iniquity, or for any sin, in any sin that he sinneth: at the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established.
Against an elder receive not an accusation, but before two or three witnesses.

Behold, here I am: witness against me before the LORD, and before his anointed: whose ox have I taken? or whose ass have I taken? or whom have I defrauded? whom have I oppressed? or of whose hand have I received any bribe to blind mine eyes therewith? and I will restore it you.
Pro 25:5
Take away the wicked from before the king, and his throne shall be established in righteousness.
corruption_summary: Impeachment is now often treated as removal itself, or as a political weapon, rather than an accusation that must be tried on evidence.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster kept two steps apart: one house accuses, the other tries and determines. Common speech now says a man was impeached as if that meant convicted or removed.
Scripture’s rule is that an accusation stands or falls on witnesses (Deu 19:15). A charge brought for faction rather than for real maladministration breaks that rule.
roots_summary: An accusation against an officer, to be tried on evidence by witnesses.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): a charge against a public officer for maladministration.
Webster: the house impeaches; the senate tries.
Two or three witnesses establish a matter (Deu 19:15).
Against an elder receive not an accusation but before witnesses (1Ti 5:19).

etymology: Webster (1828): [Latin from miles, a soldier.] He adds Greek and Hebrew comparisons that the live text prints without the original letters; this entry does not reproduce them.
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines the militia as “the body of soldiers in a state enrolled for discipline, but not engaged in actual service except in emergencies.” They are “the able bodied men organized into companies, regiments and brigades,” who at other times are “left to pursue their usual occupations.” Israel’s host was numbered the same way: “all that are able to go forth to war in Israel” (Num 1:3). Nehemiah set the builders of the wall to guard it and told them, “fight for your brethren, your sons, and your daughters, your wives, and your houses” (Neh 4:14). The law also sent home the fearful and the newly married (Deu 20:8; Deu 24:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): MILITIA, the body of soldiers in a state enrolled for discipline but not in actual service except in emergencies; able-bodied men organized and left to their usual occupations.
webster_full: MILI'TIA, noun [Latin from miles, a soldier; Gr. war, to fight, combat, contention. The primary sense of fighting is to strive, struggle, drive, or to strike, to beat, Eng. moil, Latin molior; Heb. to labor or toil.] The body of soldiers in a state enrolled for discipline, but not engaged in actual service except in emergencies; as distinguished from regular troops, whose sole occupation is war or military service. The militia of a country are the able bodied men organized into companies, regiments and brigades, with officers of all grades, and required by law to attend military exercises on certain days only, but at other times left to pursue their usual occupations.
scriptures: Num 1:3
From twenty years old and upward, all that are able to go forth to war in Israel: thou and Aaron shall number them by their armies.
Neh 4:14

And I looked, and rose up, and said unto the nobles, and to the rulers, and to the rest of the people, Be not ye afraid of them: remember the Lord, which is great and terrible, and fight for your brethren, your sons, and your daughters, your wives, and your houses.
Deu 20:8

And the officers shall speak further unto the people, and they shall say, What man is there that is fearful and fainthearted ? let him go and return unto his house, lest his brethren's heart faint as well as his heart.
Deu 24:5
When a man hath taken a new wife, he shall not go out to war, neither shall he be charged with any business: but he shall be free at home one year, and shall cheer up his wife which he hath taken.
corruption_summary: Militia now suggests a private armed band; Webster meant the lawful, enrolled body of a state’s citizens.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster set the militia against “regular troops, whose sole occupation is war.” Modern use often means an unofficial armed group, which is nearly the reverse.
Scripture’s pattern is the household defender called up in need, who fights for brethren, wives and houses and then goes home (Neh 4:14).
roots_summary: Citizens enrolled and drilled, called to arms only in emergencies.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): soldiers enrolled for discipline, not in service except in emergencies.
Webster: able bodied men, at other times left to their usual occupations.
All that are able to go forth to war (Num 1:3).
Fight for your brethren and your houses (Neh 4:14).

biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines veto as “a forbidding; prohibition; or the right of forbidding,” applied to the right of a king or magistrate “to withhold his assent to the enactment of a law, or the passing of a decree.” Scripture shows both uses of such a power. A father could annul a daughter’s vow: “But if her father disallow her in the day that he heareth” (Num 30:5). Persia’s law had no veto at all, for what was sealed with the king’s ring “may no man reverse” (Est 8:8). Over every human law stands God’s own: “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): VETO, a forbidding; the right of a king or magistrate to withhold assent to a law or decree.
webster_full: VE'TO, noun [Latin veto I forbid.] A forbidding; prohibition; or the right of forbidding; applied to the right of a king or other magistrate or officer to withhold his assent to the enactment of a law, or the passing of a decree. Thus the king of Great Britain has a veto upon every act of parliament; he sometimes prevents the passing of a law by his vet.
scriptures: Num 30:5

But if her father disallow her in the day that he heareth; not any of her vows, or of her bonds wherewith she hath bound her soul, shall stand: and the LORD shall forgive her, because her father disallowed her.
Est 8:8

Write ye also for the Jews, as it liketh you, in the king's name, and seal it with the king's ring: for the writing which is written in the king's name, and sealed with the king's ring, may no man reverse.
Dan 6:8
Now, O king, establish the decree, and sign the writing, that it be not changed, according to the law of the Medes and Persians, which altereth not.
Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
corruption_summary: Veto is now used for any refusal at all, and the sense of a lawful office withholding assent is thinned out.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster’s veto belongs to an office: a king, magistrate or officer whose assent a law requires. Casual speech uses it for any no.
The Persian law that no man could reverse shows the danger of a decree with no check (Est 8:8; Dan 6:8). A lawful veto is one such check.
roots_summary: Latin “I forbid”: an officer’s right to withhold assent from a law.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): the right of forbidding.
Webster: to withhold assent to the enactment of a law.
A father might disallow a vow (Num 30:5).
The king’s sealed writing no man may reverse (Est 8:8).

pos: n. (the number competent to transact business)
etymology: Webster (1828): [Latin gen. plural of qui, who.]
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines quorum as “such a number of officers or members as is competent by law or constitution to transact business; as a quorum of the house of representatives.” His example: “A constitutional quorum was not present.” The idea is that a body acts only when enough of it is present. When the church weighed a hard question, “the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter” (Act 15:6). Before the choice of Matthias “the number of names together were about an hundred and twenty” (Act 1:15). “In the multitude of counsellors there is safety” (Pro 11:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): QUORUM, the number of officers or members competent by law to transact business; a special commission of justices.
webster_full: QUO'RUM, noun [Latin gen. plural of qui, who.]

1. A bench of justices, or such a number of officers or members as is competent by law or constitution to transact business; as a quorum of the house of representatives. A constitutional quorum was not present.
2. A special commission of justices.
scriptures: Act 15:6
And the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter.
Act 1:15
And in those days Peter stood up in the midst of the disciples, and said, (the number of names together were about an hundred and twenty,)
Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety.
For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them.
corruption_summary: Quorum keeps its sense today; the corruption is in practice, when business is done without the body lawfully present.
corruption_paragraphs: The word is stable, but Webster’s phrase “competent by law or constitution” is the point: a decision taken without a quorum is not the body’s decision.
Scripture’s councils gathered openly and decided together (Act 15:6, 22). Counsel taken in a corner by a few is the opposite.
roots_summary: Latin, of whom: enough members present to act lawfully.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): the number competent by law to transact business.
Webster: A constitutional quorum was not present.
The apostles and elders came together (Act 15:6).
In the multitude of counsellors there is safety (Pro 11:14).
usage: a quorum of the house of representatives

pos: n. (investing an alien with a citizen’s rights)
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines naturalization as “the act of investing an alien with the rights and privileges of a native subject or citizen.” In the United States, he notes, “it is by act of Congress.” Israel’s law made room for the stranger who joined the covenant: “when a stranger shall sojourn with thee, and will keep the passover to the LORD, let all his males be circumcised” (Exo 12:48). Ruth’s vow is the heart of it: “thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God” (Rut 1:16). Paul knew the difference between a bought citizenship and a born one (Act 22:28). The gospel gives the higher grant: “ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints” (Eph 2:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): NATURALIZATION, the act of investing an alien with the rights and privileges of a native subject or citizen; in the United States, by act of Congress.
webster_full: NATURALIZATION, noun [See Naturalize] The act of investing an alien with the rights and privileges of a native subject or citizen. naturalization in Great Britain is only by act of parliament. In the United States, it is by act of Congress, vesting certain tribunals with the power.
scriptures: And when a stranger shall sojourn with thee, and will keep the passover to the LORD, let all his males be circumcised, and then let him come near and keep it; and he shall be as one that is born in the land: for no uncircumcised person shall eat thereof.
Rut 1:16

And Ruth said, Intreat me not to leave thee, or to return from following after thee: for whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God:
And the chief captain answered, With a great sum obtained I this freedom. And Paul said, But I was free born.
Eph 2:19
Now therefore ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints, and of the household of God;
corruption_summary: Naturalization is now often treated as paperwork alone; Webster’s phrase is about rights granted by lawful authority, and Scripture adds the joining of a people.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster’s definition is a legal act: an alien is invested with rights by the lawful authority. Modern talk can reduce it to a form and a fee, or blur it with simple residence.
Ruth shows what belonging meant in Israel: a new people and a new God (Rut 1:16). The church’s fellowcitizenship is given in Christ, not earned (Eph 2:19).
roots_summary: An alien invested with a native’s rights by lawful act.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): investing an alien with the rights of a citizen.
Webster: in the United States, by act of Congress.
Thy people shall be my people (Rut 1:16).
No more strangers and foreigners (Eph 2:19).
usage: the rights and privileges of a native subject or citizen

etymology: Webster (1828): [Latin]. The live text gives no further etymology; this entry does not supply one.
biblical_def: Webster (1828) gives two senses of conscription: “An enrolling or registering,” and “Soldiers or forces levied by enrolling.” Samuel warned Israel that a king would do this: “He will take your sons, and appoint them for himself, for his chariots” (1Sa 8:11). Saul did it: “when Saul saw any strong man, or any valiant man, he took him unto him” (1Sa 14:52). God’s own law set limits on the levy. The man with a new house, a new vineyard, or a new wife was sent home, and so was the fearful (Deu 20:5–8; Deu 24:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): CONSCRIPTION, an enrolling or registering; soldiers or forces levied by enrolling.
webster_full: CONSCRIPTION, noun [Latin]
1. An enrolling or registering.
2. Soldiers or forces levied by enrolling.
scriptures: And he said, This will be the manner of the king that shall reign over you: He will take your sons, and appoint them for himself, for his chariots, and to be his horsemen; and some shall run before his chariots.
And there was sore war against the Philistines all the days of Saul: and when Saul saw any strong man, or any valiant man, he took him unto him.
Deu 20:8

And the officers shall speak further unto the people, and they shall say, What man is there that is fearful and fainthearted ? let him go and return unto his house, lest his brethren's heart faint as well as his heart.
Deu 24:5
When a man hath taken a new wife, he shall not go out to war, neither shall he be charged with any business: but he shall be free at home one year, and shall cheer up his wife which he hath taken.
corruption_summary: Conscription now means only a compulsory draft; Webster’s first sense, a simple enrolling or register, is gone.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster put “an enrolling or registering” first, and the levy second. Modern use keeps only the levy.
Scripture neither forbids nor praises every levy. It records a king who took sons for himself (1Sa 8:11) and a law that exempted the newly married and the fainthearted (Deu 20:8; Deu 24:5).
roots_summary: Latin enrolling: names written down, then soldiers levied by that roll.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): an enrolling or registering.
Webster: soldiers or forces levied by enrolling.
He will take your sons (1Sa 8:11).
The fearful and fainthearted return home (Deu 20:8).
usage: Soldiers or forces levied by enrolling

biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines interposition as “a being, placing or coming between; intervention,” and as “intervenient agency; as the interposition of the magistrate in quieting sedition.” He gives a theological example: “How many evidences have we of divine interposition in favor of good men!” and a third sense, “Mediation; agency between parties.” Aaron interposed for a guilty people: “he stood between the dead and the living; and the plague was stayed” (Num 16:48). Moses “stood before him in the breach, to turn away his wrath” (Psa 106:23). The final interposition is Christ’s: “there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1Ti 2:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): INTERPOSITION, a coming between; intervention; intervenient agency, as of a magistrate or of God; mediation between parties.
webster_full: INTERPOSI'TION, noun [Latin interpositio.]

1. A being, placing or coming between; intervention; as the interposition of the Baltic sea between Germany and Sweden. The interposition of the moon between the earth and the sun occasions a solar eclipse.
2. Intervenient agency; as the interposition of the magistrate in quieting sedition. How many evidences have we of divine interposition in favor of good men!
3. Mediation; agency between parties. By the interposition of a common friend, the parties have been reconciled.
4. Any thing interposed.
scriptures: And he stood between the dead and the living; and the plague was stayed.
Therefore he said that he would destroy them, had not Moses his chosen stood before him in the breach, to turn away his wrath, lest he should destroy them.
For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus;
And I sought for a man among them, that should make up the hedge, and stand in the gap before me for the land, that I should not destroy it: but I found none.
corruption_summary: Interposition is now heard mostly as a disputed term of states’ rights; Webster’s wider sense of mediation and divine intervention is forgotten.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster’s senses run from an eclipse to a magistrate to the providence of God. In modern American use the word is mostly tied to one constitutional dispute, and the rest drops out.
Scripture’s great interposition is mediation: one who stands between wrath and the guilty (Num 16:48; 1Ti 2:5). This entry does not take a side on the constitutional doctrine.
roots_summary: A placing between: intervention, mediation, standing in the breach.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): a being, placing or coming between.
Webster: divine interposition in favor of good men.
Webster: mediation; agency between parties.
He stood between the dead and the living (Num 16:48).
One mediator between God and men (1Ti 2:5).
usage: the interposition of the magistrate in quieting sedition

pos: n. phrase (unwritten law of long usage)
etymology: Webster’s own phrase, under LAW, sense 11: “Unwritten or common law.”
biblical_def: Webster (1828), under LAW, defines “unwritten or common law” as “a rule of action which derives its authority from long usage, or established custom, which has been immemorially received and recognized by judicial tribunals.” Because it “can be traced to no positive statutes,” its rules “are to be found only in the records of courts, and in the reports of judicial decisions.” Scripture honours settled usage that is just: “Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set” (Pro 22:28); “ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein” (Jer 6:16). Custom is not its own warrant. The Gentiles show “the work of the law written in their hearts” (Rom 2:15), and every custom answers to God’s law.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), LAW sense 11: unwritten or common law, a rule of action deriving authority from long usage and custom, found in court records and reported decisions.
webster_full: 11. Unwritten or common law a rule of action which derives its authority from long usage, or established custom, which has been immemorially received and recognized by judicial tribunals. As this law can be traced to no positive statutes, its rules or principles are to be found only in the records of courts, and in the reports of judicial decisions.
scriptures: Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set.
Jer 6:16
Thus saith the LORD, Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls. But they said, We will not walk therein.
Rom 2:15
Which shew the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience also bearing witness, and their thoughts the mean while accusing or else excusing one another;)
Mar 7:8
For laying aside the commandment of God, ye hold the tradition of men, as the washing of pots and cups: and many other such like things ye do.
corruption_summary: Common law is now often treated as judge-made law that may change at will, rather than custom received and recognized from time out of mind.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster’s common law is received, not invented: authority from “long usage, or established custom.” Modern talk can make it mean whatever courts decide this year.
Scripture’s old landmark and old paths value what the fathers set (Pro 22:28; Jer 6:16), but only where it is the good way. A custom against God’s law is not made right by age (Mar 7:8).
roots_summary: Law by long usage, received from time out of mind and kept in court records.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): a rule of action from long usage, or established custom.
Webster: traced to no positive statutes.
Remove not the ancient landmark (Pro 22:28).
Ask for the old paths, where is the good way (Jer 6:16).
